author: Chhavi Gupta
text:
Recruiters don't search for the best engineer.

They search for the most visible one.

If your LinkedIn profile doesn't clearly communicate your expertise, you're missing opportunities before the interview even begins.

Here are 7 simple ways to attract HRs to your LinkedIn profile:

1. Write a Clear Headline

Don't just write "Telecom Engineer."

Instead, explain what you do.

Example:
5G Core Engineer | O-RAN | IMS | Cloud-Native Telecom | Open to Opportunities

2. Optimize Your About Section

Tell your story.

Highlight:

• Your experience
• Your technical expertise
• The problems you solve
• The value you bring

3. Use the Right Keywords

Recruiters search using keywords.

Include technologies such as:

• 5G NR
• LTE
• O-RAN
• IMS
• VoLTE
• VoNR
• Kubernetes
• DevOps
• Cloud
• AI/ML

4. Showcase Measurable Achievements

Don't just list responsibilities.

Show results.

For example:

• Reduced call drop rate by 20%
• Automated 500+ test cases
• Led 5G deployment across multiple sites
• Improved network KPIs

Numbers build credibility.

5. Stay Active

A profile that's active gets noticed.

Share:

• Technical insights
• Industry news
• Lessons learned
• Infographics
• Project experiences

Consistency builds visibility.

6. Build a Strong Network

Connect with:

• Recruiters
• Hiring Managers
• Telecom Leaders
• Engineers
• Industry Experts

Networking creates opportunities that job portals often miss.

7. Turn On "Open to Work"

Let recruiters know you're available.

This simple setting increases your chances of appearing in recruiter searches.

Quick Wins

• Use a professional profile photo
• Create a strong LinkedIn banner
• Optimize your Featured section
• Post consistently
• Engage with your network

Recruiter Tip

A great LinkedIn profile answers four questions immediately:

• Who are you?
• What do you do?
• What technologies do you specialize in?
• Why should someone contact you?

If your profile answers these questions clearly, you're already ahead of most candidates.

author: Ashok Kumar Rapaka, open to work
text:
💡 "They know AI" means very different things right now — and most job posts and resumes don't make the distinction.
Every week I see this mismatch: a recruiter posts "AI Engineer needed" and can't tell if a Copilot user for 6 months qualifies — or a candidate with real LLM/RAG/agent experience gets rejected because their resume reads the same as someone who just enabled Copilot in VS Code.
Here's the honest breakdown — 4 real tiers of "AI skill" today:
🟢 Tier 1 — AI tool user: Using Copilot or ChatGPT to code faster. Baseline in 2026, not a differentiator.
🟡 Tier 2 — AI-integrated developer: Connecting an LLM API into a real app — sending prompts, handling responses.
🟠 Tier 3 — RAG & agentic AI builder: Vector search, multi-step agents that call tools on their own, MCP integration. This is where real differentiation is.
🔴 Tier 4 — AI/ML model builder: Training or fine-tuning actual models. Needed for very few roles.
For experienced developers and testers: you don't need to become a Tier 4 researcher. Most companies hiring right now need Tier 2 and 3 — and your existing skills in system design, API integration, and debugging transfer directly. Learn LLM integration, RAG, and tool-calling patterns, and apply the same rigor you already have.
For recruiters: before writing "AI Engineer," ask — do we need a tool user, an integrator, an agent builder, or a model trainer? That one question prevents hiring the wrong tier entirely.
What tier are you in right now — or hiring for? 👇

If you are a tech professional on H-1B · 
Read this today. Not next week.

The US tech job market changed structurally in 2026. 
Most engineers on H-1B still haven't processed what happened. 

Here is the honest 2026 reality check · every policy shift · every company move · with the numbers 👇

📉 𝐖𝐡𝐚𝐭 𝐇𝐚𝐩𝐩𝐞𝐧𝐞𝐝 𝐭𝐨 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐌𝐚𝐫𝐤𝐞𝐭
→ 120K+ tech roles cut in 2026 (as of July)
→ 56% of layoff events cite AI as a driver
→ General software engineering postings down 49% vs 2020 baseline
→ ML engineer openings up 59% vs 2020 baseline
↳ Two markets now · not one. AI up · average roles down.

💰 𝐓𝐡𝐞 𝐬𝟏𝟎𝟎𝐊 𝐇-𝟏𝐁 𝐅𝐞𝐞
→ Trump proclamation added a $100,000 fee to H-1B applications
→ Only ~85 payments of the fee by mid-February 2026
→ JPMorgan projects 66,000 FEWER work authorizations per year
↳ The fee alone chilled sponsorship for smaller + mid-cap employers.

🎲 𝐓𝐡𝐞 𝐖𝐚𝐠𝐞-𝐖𝐞𝐢𝐠𝐡𝐭𝐞𝐝 𝐋𝐨𝐭𝐭𝐞𝐫𝐲 (𝐅𝐘 𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟕)
→ Random lottery is GONE. Replaced with wage-weighted selection.
→ Level IV (highest wage) = 4 lottery entries
→ Level III = 3 · Level II = 2 · Level I = 1 entry
→ Independent modeling: Level I odds ~10-12% · Level IV ~65-70%
↳ Entry-level + "average" roles just took the biggest hit in H-1B history.

🏢 𝐂𝐨𝐦𝐩𝐚𝐧𝐢𝐞𝐬 𝐓𝐡𝐚𝐭 𝐏𝐀𝐔𝐒𝐄𝐃 / 𝐒𝐓𝐎𝐏𝐏𝐄𝐃

→ Walmart · ~2,400 H-1B holders · paused new H-1B sponsorship
→ Cognizant · listings say "must be authorized without sponsorship"
→ Intuitive Surgical · notices on 100+ job listings · no sponsorship
↳ These aren't small companies. The pattern is corporate policy shift.

🏆 𝐂𝐨𝐦𝐩𝐚𝐧𝐢𝐞𝐬 𝐒𝐭𝐢𝐥𝐥 𝐒𝐩𝐨𝐧𝐬𝐨𝐫𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐀𝐠𝐠𝐫𝐞𝐬𝐬𝐢𝐯𝐞𝐥𝐲
→ Amazon: 10,044 H-1B approvals FY 2025 · avg salary $157K
→ Microsoft · Google · Meta · Apple · direct hire still active
→ AI-first companies (OpenAI · Anthropic · Databricks · scale-up ML)
↳ All predominantly filing at Level III / IV wages.

📊 𝐓𝐡𝐞 𝐍𝐞𝐰 𝐌𝐚𝐫𝐤𝐞𝐭 𝐒𝐡𝐚𝐩𝐞

↳ Hiring didn't stop. It filtered. Level IV wages + specialized skills win.

~ Assuming H-1B lottery is still "random" (it isn't)

The Micro-World continuously evolves as people and AI learn from one another while solving the problem together.

That's how we believe frontier problems should be solved.

This Biomarker Discovery Micro-World is one example of what we build at 1st Principles AI.

I used to think the talent gap was just about hiring more people. Turns out, it's way more nuanced than that.

The BFSI and NBFC sectors are facing a HUGE talent shortage, as highlighted in a recent Economic Times piece. These are the people who drive innovation forward.

And the impact? It's massive. Without these skills, innovation stalls. Companies struggle to adopt new technologies, personalize customer experiences, or even manage risk effectively in today's rapidly changing financial landscape. This isn't just a minor inconvenience; it directly hinders growth and competitiveness.

So, what's the playbook to bridge this gap?

1.  Targeted Upskilling & Reskilling: Forget generic training. Companies need to invest in niche programs focused on the exact skills in demand.
2.  Strategic Partnerships: Collaborating with universities and specialized tech bootcamps is crucial. 
3.  Embrace Internal Talent: Promote and train existing employees. Often, the passion and company knowledge are already there; they just need the specialized skills.

This isn't just about recruitment; it's about strategic talent development. The BFSI firms that prioritize this will not only survive but thrive.
